summary: Defines procedures for allocating and retiring special-purpose MPLS labels, which come from a small set of 16, and a way to extend the special-purpose label space. It renames the IANA registry and creates an Extended Special-Purpose MPLS Label Values registry. It updates several earlier RFCs that use the term reserved label.

plainLanguage.summary: There are only 16 special tags and they are nearly used up. This document sets rules for handing out and taking back tags, and makes a way to have more.

questions: what is the mpls extension label
how is a special-purpose mpls label retired
subtitle: Rules for handing out and retiring the 16 special MPLS labels, plus a way to get more of them.

tldr.problem: Only 16 MPLS label values (0 to 15) are set aside as special-purpose labels, and 9 were still unassigned, so they are scarce and costly to change in forwarding hardware.
tldr.mechanism: Allocation of special-purpose labels is by Standards Action, a strict process is defined for deprecating and retiring one, and label 15 becomes the Extension Label (XL), which is followed by an Extended Special-Purpose Label (ESPL) from a new, larger registry.
tldr.outcome: The IANA registry is renamed and a new Extended Special-Purpose MPLS Label Values registry is created. The RFC updates 13 earlier RFCs, and it has itself been updated by RFC 9017.

today: RFC 7274 is a Standards Track document that has been updated by RFC 9017. It has not been obsoleted, and it updates RFC 3032 and twelve other RFCs.

sections.title: The Scarcity of Special-Purpose Labels
sections.content:
RFC 3032 defined four special-purpose label values (0 to 3) and set aside values 4 through 15 for future use. Since then, three more have been allocated (7, 13 and 14), so nine values from the original sixteen remain unassigned.

The RFC says the concern is not the pace of allocation but the scarcity. Many special-purpose labels need special processing by forwarding hardware, which is often expensive and sometimes impossible to change, so documenting a newly allocated value matters. The block 0 to 15 was commonly called "reserved labels"; this document calls them special-purpose labels.
sections.plainLanguage: There are only a few special stickers, and changing how machines read a sticker is hard, so each new one must be written down carefully.

sections.title: Allocation Policy and the Six Questions
sections.content:
The RFC poses six questions and answers each. The allocation answers are:

  • Allocation of special-purpose labels is via Standards Action, so a Standards Track RFC must accompany a request.
  • The IANA registry is renamed "Special-Purpose MPLS Label Values".
  • Early allocation may be allowed case by case.
  • The space of 16 is too small for experimental or private use, but the new extended registry has enough space and defines a range for experimental use.

On the Implicit NULL Label (value 3), which is only used in signaling, the answer is that data-plane use is not allowed for now. Revisiting that would need a Standards Track RFC that explains the use, discusses confusion between signaling and data plane, and mitigates it.
sections.plainLanguage: New special stickers need a proper, well-reviewed document first. Sticker number 3 stays a signal-only sticker for now.

sections.title: The Extension Label and Extended Labels
sections.content:
Label value 15 is set aside as the Extension Label (XL). The XL MUST be followed by another label L, so it MUST have the bottom-of-stack bit clear. L is interpreted as an Extended Special-Purpose Label (ESPL) using the new registry. The XL only gives special meaning to L; a label after L is parsed as usual and may be a regular label or a special-purpose label, including another XL followed by another ESPL.

Values 0 to 15 of the extended registry are reserved. Values 0-6 and 8-15 MUST NOT appear in the data plane after an XL, and an LSR that sees an XL on top of the stack followed by one of those values MUST drop the packet.

Label 7, the Entropy Label Indicator (ELI), keeps its meaning whether it is a regular label or an ESPL, for backward compatibility with deployed code and hardware. When an LSR inserts an entropy label, it MUST insert the ELI as a regular special-purpose label, not as an ESPL.
sections.plainLanguage: Sticker 15 means 'look at the next sticker, it comes from the big box'. The big box has its own rules about which stickers are allowed.

sections.title: Forwarding, Load Balancing and Choosing a Label
sections.content:
If an LSR sees the XL at the top of the stack and does not understand extension labels, it MUST drop the packet, as for an invalid incoming label under RFC 3031. The same applies to an ESPL it does not understand. The LSR MAY log the event, but logging MUST be rate-limited. An LSR SHOULD NOT make forwarding decisions on labels that are not at the top of the stack.

RFC 6790 says special-purpose labels MUST NOT be used for load balancing, and this document applies the same rule to ESPLs. The RFC notes that existing implementations would violate this, because they treat the XL as a single special-purpose label and do not expect an ESPL to follow. The consequence is that packets of one flow could take different paths and be re-ordered.

When allocating a new special-purpose label, designers should consider an ESPL first, to save the scarce regular values for cases where keeping the label stack small is particularly important.
sections.plainLanguage: A machine that does not know the big-box signal throws the packet away. Packets with these stickers should not be split across different roads, because they might arrive out of order.

sections.title: Retiring a Special-Purpose Label
sections.content:
The RFC says retiring a label is difficult and the process should be used sparingly. It has three steps.

  • A label may be deprecated by IETF consensus with review by the MPLS working group (or designated experts). An RFC with at least Informational status is required. IANA marks the value "deprecated" but does not release it. Vendors should not use it in new implementations, and operators should avoid it in new deployments.
  • Twelve months after that RFC, an IETF-wide survey may check whether the value is still in use, and may be repeated after an additional 6 months.
  • If the survey shows it is not in use, then 24 months after the deprecating RFC, a Standards Track Internet-Draft may be requested to retire the value. That document asks IANA to release it for future assignment.
sections.plainLanguage: Taking back a sticker is slow on purpose. First say it is going away, then ask everyone if they still use it, and only then give it away again.

sections.title: IANA Actions and Updated RFCs
sections.content:
IANA renamed the "Multiprotocol Label Switching Architecture (MPLS) Label Values" registry to "Special-Purpose MPLS Label Values", changed its policy to Standards Action, and assigned value 15 as the "Extension Label". It created the "Extended Special-Purpose MPLS Label Values" registry, also by Standards Action, with the ranges below. Early allocation under RFC 7120 is allowed only for values assigned by Standards Action.

Thirteen earlier RFCs use the term "reserved labels", including RFC 3032, RFC 3209, RFC 5586 and RFC 6790. This document updates them, and all such references should be read as "special-purpose labels".
sections.plainLanguage: The list keeper gave the old list a new name, made the new big list, and every old document that said 'reserved' now means 'special-purpose'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document does not greatly change the MPLS data plane, so security considerations are largely those of the MPLS architecture (RFC 3031) and the MPLS and GMPLS security framework (RFC 5920).

There are two cautions. Inserting additional {XL, ESPL} pairs is a protocol-legal way to grow the label stack faster than inserting single rogue labels, which might be used to attack nodes that can process only stacks of a certain size. Larger stacks can also cause fragmentation or make packets unprocessable by some implementations. Second, some events may cause an LSR to log at a per-packet rate, so implementations MUST rate-limit such logs.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could pile on lots of extra stickers to overload a slow machine, and a machine must not write a complaint for every single packet.
